newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's Lee done enough on Malaysia spat -analysts.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's Lee done enough on Malaysia spat -analysts.

text.p: Singapore elder statesman Lee Kuan Yew has gone as far as he can to end a diplomatic row over his criticism of Malaysia, analysts said on Tuesday, although some said they thought his latest effort lacked sincerity.

Lee said in a statement on Monday he would ask a local court to delete a remark in an affidavit that the Malaysian state of Johor "was notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings," a blast that infuriated Kuala Lumpur.
"I think he has done everything that he can reasonably do short of saying, yes I believe that Johor is an extremely safe place," former member of parliament Walter Woon told Reuters.
"The Malaysians asked for an apology, he has apologised, he has taken it off the record. What else do you want him to say?"
Woon said the issue was not between Singapore and Malaysia because "it's Lee Kuan Yew's personal opinion...it has got nothing to do with the rest of us."

Last week, in a statement from his press secretary, Lee apologised unreservedly for the remark, made in pursuit of a libel action against an opposition Singapore politician who fled to Johor and which he had not expected to become public.

The Malaysian Foreign Ministry demanded a retraction. Some Malaysians demonstrated, carrying placards insulting Lee. Some even demanded a revision of Malaysia's relations with its tiny but economically powerful neighbour.

However, the immediate reaction to Lee's statement on Monday suggested Woon could be right in saying that Lee's latest statement should satisfy Malaysia, where Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim described it as more positive than the apology.
Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said plainly at the weekend that Lee was "offside", or in the wrong, in criticising Johor.
"We have discussed this, but basically he doesn't retract statements based on perceptions," Goh said.
A political scientist said: "Offside means you are breaking the rules of the game. Clearly the apportionment of blame is on this side."
Woon said it would to be hard to make a full retraction of something involved in a court case. "It's hard to unsay what has already been said."
A lawyer who declined to be named said he did not consider Lee's promise to have the offending phrases deleted from the court record as a retraction.
"It's a very half-hearted thing. The Malaysians are requiring a retraction and even his apology is very half hearted," the lawyer said.
He said some sections of Malaysia's ruling party would not "let the matter go" until Lee went further.
But a political scientist familiar with Singapore-Malaysia relations said the deletion of the offending remarks could be seen as a retraction "because the affidavit has to be refiled".
Several letters to Singapore's Straits Times newspaper called for calm.

"Mr Lee's remarks might not be representative," Seow Poh Leong wrote. "It would be most unfortunate if such an incident should cause repercussions for business relations between the two countries...or worse create animosity between the two peoples."
Other letter writers said Lee's remark about Johor being unsafe was not totally without substance, citing recent newspaper reports of Singaporeans being robbed and murdered.
